A Bloomberg report claims Apple Glasses may launch without photo or video capabilities. Reportedly, Apple is considering this approach to address external privacy concerns.

However, while I completely understand why Apple would consider this option, based on my personal experience using Ray-Ban Meta glasses, the video recording function is absolutely the core feature of this type of product...

Privacy considerations have driven many of Apple's decisions, and remain a major selling point of their ecosystem.

For example, with AI features, the company keeps as much computation as possible on-device. When cloud computing is required, "Private Cloud Compute" is designed to ensure Apple cannot access user data, while allowing security researchers to verify this independently. This is undoubtedly a good thing.

Privacy Concerns Around Smart Glasses

Undeniably, smart glasses equipped with video recording do raise privacy concerns. One of the main reasons Google Glass failed was precisely this — its wearers earned the unflattering nickname "Glassholes."

Ray-Ban Meta glasses have similarly sparked privacy controversies, partly because some YouTubers used them in a deeply offensive manner, as noted in earlier BBC News coverage.

The company also faced criticism after it was exposed that sensitive video clips (including accidental recordings) were being sent to human data annotators.

For all these reasons, I completely understand why Apple would have reservations about adding video recording to Apple Glasses.

But Video Recording Is the Key Feature

Apple's dilemma is that video recording is now an important feature of smart glasses, and based on my own usage, I wouldn't even consider wearing them without it.

Let me list the various features of Ray-Ban Meta, then share my experience using them:

  • Ask Meta AI about what you're looking at
  • Play music
  • Hands-free voice calls — making and receiving
  • Receive voice notifications, including having incoming messages read aloud
  • Capture first-person photos via button or voice command
  • Capture first-person videos via button or voice command

Ask questions of the AI

Meta lists this as one of the main reasons to buy the glasses, and admittedly, the first impression is genuinely impressive. For example, you can look at a famous landmark and ask the glasses to tell you about it. They can also recognise many different objects, from flowers to sculptures. It's like having Apple Intelligence with you everywhere, without having to pull out your iPhone.

When I first got them, I tested these features thoroughly and felt excited about future applications. I imagined being able to look at nearby restaurants and have the glasses automatically tell me each one's average TripAdvisor rating and what previous diners had recommended.

However, as things stand now, I almost never use this feature, and it certainly isn't enough to make me wear smart glasses daily.

Playing Music

There's no way around it: with tiny speakers mounted on the temple arms, the sound quality simply isn't good enough. Headphones will always be the better choice, and earbuds are equally convenient.

Hands-free Voice Calls

Being able to take a quick call or two while cycling can occasionally be useful, because I don't want to wear in-ear headphones that block out ambient sound. But once the conversation runs longer than a few sentences, I'll always stop first, so this alone simply isn't enough to make me wear smart glasses daily.

Voice Notifications

I'm quite fond of this feature. If a text comes in, whether via iMessage or WhatsApp, the glasses can read it out to me while I'm walking or cycling. But again, this benefit alone isn't enough to justify buying them.

Photos and Videos

Honestly, this is the biggest selling point of current smart glasses. Being able to capture first-person video without having to hold a phone is fantastic — not just for special experiences like riding a rollercoaster or sailing, but also for revisiting holiday or weekend sightseeing trips. As I wrote in my initial Ray-Ban Meta glasses review:

I've also found it a great way to film cycling videos. Since I'm already wearing sunglasses anyway, pressing a button on the glasses is far more convenient than mounting a camera on the bike. My motorcycling friends use the same method.

This is the biggest reason I wear them, and if this benefit were removed, I honestly wouldn't bother. I believe an Apple Glasses without photo and video capabilities would be pointless to release. (The situation is different for smart glasses equipped with displays — I'll share my experience with those in a later article, but the first-generation Apple Glasses are not expected to have this design.)

What Should Apple Do?

Fortunately, I don't think finding a balance between practicality and privacy is impossible.

One criticism of Ray-Ban Meta glasses is that while they have an LED indicator that flashes when recording, it's not very visible in strong sunlight. Apple could ensure their own LED is designed for high visibility.

Featured Comment from CCATX

I don't entirely agree with Ben's take here. I admit I may not be the target audience for this product — I never had any intention of buying Meta glasses, and I'm not particularly interested in whatever Apple eventually releases either. But I know one thing for sure: many people are already deeply annoyed at being photographed and filmed in public without their knowledge. This is the strongest backlash I've seen against products like Ring doorbells and Meta glasses. It's now reached the point where museums, entertainment venues, and other businesses are considering banning glasses equipped with recording devices. Whatever path Apple ultimately takes with their smart glasses, the responsibility lies with them — to convince consumers either that it's worth buying without cameras, or that the benefits of having them outweigh the drawbacks. For me, either route will take considerable effort to be convinced.

Apple could also place speakers on the outer side of the temple arms that play audible cues when recording starts or stops, alerting those nearby. Another approach would be to remove physical photo/video buttons entirely and force users to operate the function via voice commands only. Both methods would make it clear to people around the wearer that they are being recorded.

Of course, there's no perfect solution here. There will always be someone who can start recording from a distance and only move closer to the target afterward. But I believe combining several privacy protection features would be effective in the vast majority of situations.

The standard Apple needs to meet isn't perfection — it's making abuse difficult enough that those with ill intent won't choose this product.

What are your thoughts on this dilemma? Feel free to share your views in the comments.
